title: Disabled admin: time, structural barriers, and the degree awarding gap in undergraduate chemistry
content: Disabled students represent approximately 15–19% of the undergraduate population in higher education globally, yet disabled chemists remain significantly underrepresented within the profession. Despite this, disability remains markedly neglected as a topic within chemistry education research. In the United Kingdom, despite a doubling of disability disclosure rates among STEM undergraduates between 2007–08 and 2018–19, disabled students continue to face a 4.4 percentage point degree awarding gap and a 4–7 percentage point employment gap compared with non-disabled peers. Discipline-specific barriers—including inaccessible laboratory equipment, sensory stressors, inconsistent implementation of disability support plans (DSPs—institutional documents outlining agreed reasonable adjustments for individual disabled students), and attitudinal resistance among teaching staff—may compound these structural disadvantages, yet these remain poorly understood at the departmental level. This study investigated the academic, social, and structural barriers reported by students with disabilities in an undergraduate and postgraduate chemistry department at Durham University, employing a sequential mixed-methods design developed collaboratively with students. An online survey (n = 56; of whom 28 (50%) self-identified as disabled) was followed by semi-structured interviews (n = 8). Thematic analysis of qualitative data, alongside descriptive statistical analysis of survey responses, revealed that disabled students frequently perceived standard accommodations as insufficiently tailored to their needs, reported significant variation in teaching staff implementation of DSPs, and identified physical laboratory inaccessibility, timetabling pressures, and limited staff awareness as potentially important barriers. Targeted institutional initiatives to address the degree awarding gap were largely unknown to participants. These findings suggest that increased disability disclosure alone may be insufficient to address participation and outcome gaps without concurrent changes to the physical, pedagogical, and attitudinal environment. The study supports consideration of chemistry-specific, structurally embedded accessibility interventions across teaching practice, assessment design, and departmental support provision.
